nameStory: Eastern Grass Shrimp earned their common name from their love of shallow, grassy waters where aquatic plants grow thick. They're also called "ghost shrimp" or "glass shrimp" because their bodies are so translucent you can see right through them, making them appear almost supernatural as they dart through the water.
description: Eastern Grass Shrimp are tiny, nearly transparent freshwater crustaceans that look like miniature versions of the shrimp you might eat for dinner. These delicate creatures have long, whisker-like antennae and swim with quick, darting movements through shallow waters. They typically grow to about 1-2 inches long and have a curved, humpbacked body that's so clear you can often see their internal organs through their shell.

idTips.label: Translucent Body
idTips.description: The body is almost completely see-through, like looking through frosted glass, allowing you to glimpse dark internal structures and sometimes food in their gut

idTips.label: Quick Darting Movement
idTips.description: They move in sudden, jerky bursts rather than smooth swimming, propelling themselves backward when startled with rapid tail flicks

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of long, thread-like antennae extend from the head, often longer than the body itself and constantly twitching to sense their surroundings

idTips.label: Curved Body Shape
idTips.description: The body has a distinctive humpbacked curve, especially noticeable when viewed from the side, giving them a comma-like silhouette

idTips.label: Swimming Legs
idTips.description: Tiny paddle-like swimming legs (pleopods) under the abdomen create a constant fluttering motion, visible as a blur beneath the translucent body

habitat: Eastern Grass Shrimp prefer shallow freshwater areas with abundant vegetation, including slow-moving streams, ponds, and marshy areas throughout New England. They're most commonly found among aquatic plants like eelgrass and pondweed, where they can hide and forage. Look for them in areas with soft, muddy or sandy bottoms where organic matter accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, with adults becoming more visible in shallow areas. Peak breeding season begins, making them easier to spot in large numbers.
seasonality.summer: At their most abundant and easiest to observe, gathering in shallow, warm waters among dense aquatic vegetation. Young shrimp appear, looking like tiny versions of adults.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters or seek shelter. Numbers may appear reduced as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, often burrowing into soft sediments or hiding deep among plant roots until spring returns.

funFact: Eastern Grass Shrimp are considered a keystone species, meaning their presence is so important that they help maintain the entire ecosystem's balance - despite being nearly invisible, these tiny creatures are ecological superheroes that keep their freshwater worlds healthy!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small aquatic invertebrates like water fleas or young fish, but the long antennae and backward-swimming escape behavior are dead giveaways. Remember: if it darts backward when disturbed and has whiskers longer than its body, it's likely a grass shrimp.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "grass shrimp," they're not the same as the marine grass shrimp sold in bait shops, and they're completely different from the larger "ghost shrimp" sold in aquarium stores, which are actually burrowing mud shrimp from saltwater environments.
compareHints: Eastern Grass Shrimp are distinguished from their close relatives like Daggerblade Grass Shrimp by their freshwater habitat preference, while Daggerblade species prefer brackish or saltwater marshes. Rockpool Prawns are found in marine tidepools rather than freshwater, and Oriental Shrimp are typically larger and found in different water conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Rockpool prawns can be distinguished from other Palaemon glass shrimp in New England by their habitat preference for rocky tide pools rather than salt marshes or estuaries.
Oriental Shrimp can be distinguished from other Palaemon species by their exceptionally long antennae and more pronounced rostrum.

Among its glass shrimp relatives, the marsh grass shrimp is the only one with those distinctive orange eyestalks — the Eastern grass shrimp lacks this coloration, while the Daggerblade grass shrimp has different body proportions.

Among its glass shrimp relatives, the daggerblade stands out with its distinctive brownish spots scattered across the transparent body - other Palaemon species in New England waters tend to be more uniformly colored or have different spot patterns.
Compared to the more common Marsh Grass Shrimp and Eastern Grass Shrimp in New England waters, Palaemon mundusnovus is distinguished by subtle differences in antenna proportions and body shape.
